claims.text: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has low hardness and strength primarily because its homogeneous simple solid-solution microstructure provides few obstacles to dislocation motion.
The starting CoCrFeNiTi state is homogeneous and consists of coarse grains without secondary strengthening phases.
Cold rolling followed by controlled annealing can refine the grains of the alloy.
Cold rolling followed by controlled annealing can produce secondary precipitates in the alloy.
The precipitates are expected to be nanoscale and located at grain boundaries or within grains.
Grain boundaries and precipitates obstruct or pin dislocations.
Increased resistance to dislocation motion from refined grains and precipitates produces greater strain hardening.
Increased resistance to dislocation motion raises yield strength and hardness.
The homogeneous baseline state permits facile dislocation glide and therefore easy plastic deformation.
Thermomechanically processed specimens should have higher yield and ultimate tensile strengths than the as-cast simple-solid-solution baseline.
Thermomechanically processed specimens should have higher hardness than the baseline.
The strength and hardness increase may be accompanied by reduced ductility.
Baseline CoCrFeNiTi combines high plasticity and machinability with low hardness and strength.
The comparison holds composition constant at equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi while changing thermomechanical history.
The hypothesis is limited to processing schedules that generate heterogeneity without detrimental grain growth or excessive precipitate coarsening.
The predicted response is limited to room-temperature tensile or hardness loading at moderate strain rates.
The quantitative property improvement depends sensitively on processing parameters and the resulting microstructure.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant hardness and yield-strength increase, or failure to observe the expected refined and precipitate-bearing microstructure, is designated as falsification.
